title: Grokking, Emergence, and What the Word Transition Is Doing
outline:
The closing chapter, and the one that must resist its own thesis hardest. Modern deep learning has revived every element of Chapter 19, in the jamming transition separating under- from over-parametrized networks, in double descent, in grokking, where a network memorizes for thousands of steps and then abruptly generalizes, and in the claim that large language models exhibit emergent abilities appearing suddenly at scale. Twice over, the abruptness has turned out to be partly in the observer. Neel Nanda, Lawrence Chan and colleagues reverse-engineered grokking and found three continuous phases underneath an apparently discontinuous curve, and Rylan Schaeffer, Brando Miranda and Sanmi Koyejo showed that many reported emergent abilities dissolve into smooth curves when a discontinuous metric such as exact-match accuracy is replaced by a continuous one, which puts the discontinuity in the ruler rather than the system. The chapter takes both counterarguments as central rather than mentioning them in passing. The book ends by asking what work the word transition is actually doing in each of its uses across the preceding nineteen chapters, and where the analogy is load-bearing rather than decorative.

Built on Geiger, Spigler, Wyart and colleagues on jamming in deep networks read against the physical jamming transition introduced in Chapter 4, Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal on double descent, Power, Burda and colleagues on grokking together with Nanda, Chan and colleagues on the three continuous phases beneath it, Wei and colleagues on emergent abilities, Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo at NeurIPS 2023, and the finite-size argument from Chapter 1 applied to model scale.

Leaves open: deliberately unresolved. The reader is left with the question the book cannot answer, which is what an order parameter for a transformer would even be, and therefore whether these systems have a phase diagram at all.

verifiedClaims.claim: John J. Hopfield introduced a recurrent network of two-state neurons with symmetric connections whose dynamics descend a Lyapunov 'energy' function identical in form to that of an Ising spin system, so that stored memories are the energy minima; this paper made statistical mechanics directly applicable to neural computation and reported an empirical storage limit of about 0.15N patterns for N neurons.
verifiedClaims.people: John J. Hopfield
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Biology, California Institute of Technology, and Bell Laboratories
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 79, no. 8, pp. 2554-2558

verifiedClaims.claim: David H. Ackley, Geoffrey E. Hinton and Terrence J. Sejnowski defined the Boltzmann machine, a network of stochastic binary units whose equilibrium states follow the Boltzmann distribution, and derived a learning rule based on the difference between correlations in a clamped 'wake' phase and a free-running 'sleep' phase — importing simulated annealing and thermal equilibrium from statistical physics into machine learning.
verifiedClaims.people: David H. Ackley, Geoffrey E. Hinton, Terrence J. Sejnowski
verifiedClaims.venue: Cognitive Science, vol. 9, no. 1, pp. 147-169

verifiedClaims.claim: Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund and Haim Sompolinsky applied replica mean-field theory to the Hopfield model in the saturation limit where the number of stored patterns p grows proportionally to network size N (p = alpha*N), and showed that despite the model's spin-glass character, dynamically stable retrieval states almost fully correlated with individual stored patterns exist below a critical load — the first analytic proof that associative memory survives as a distinct thermodynamic phase.
verifiedClaims.people: Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund, Haim Sompolinsky
verifiedClaims.affiliation: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 55, no. 14, pp. 1530-1533

verifiedClaims.claim: In the full-length treatment of the Hopfield model near saturation, Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund and Haim Sompolinsky mapped the complete phase diagram in the load-temperature plane and located the critical storage capacity at zero temperature, above which retrieval states abruptly disappear and the network enters a spin-glass phase; below the critical load the network retrieves patterns with an error of less than about 1.5 percent. This critical value, conventionally quoted as alpha_c approximately 0.138, is the canonical 'memory cliff' of associative memory.
verifiedClaims.people: Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund, Haim Sompolinsky
verifiedClaims.affiliation: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
verifiedClaims.venue: Annals of Physics, vol. 173, no. 1, pp. 30-67

verifiedClaims.claim: Elizabeth Gardner reframed neural network capacity as a question about the geometry of weight space rather than about any particular learning rule, computing the typical fractional volume of the space of couplings that correctly stores a given set of random patterns as stable states. This volume shrinks continuously to zero at a critical pattern density, and the construction — now universally called the Gardner volume — became the standard method for computing capacity in learning systems.
verifiedClaims.people: Elizabeth Gardner
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Edinburgh
verifiedClaims.venue: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General, vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 257-270

verifiedClaims.claim: Elizabeth Gardner and Bernard Derrida computed the maximum number of random patterns an optimal neural network can store as a function of the allowed fraction of bit errors and of a stability margin K, obtaining a critical line alpha_c(K) with alpha_c(0) = 2 — the celebrated result that an optimally trained perceptron can store two patterns per weight, twice the Hebbian-rule capacity.
verifiedClaims.people: Elizabeth Gardner, Bernard Derrida
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Edinburgh (Gardner)
verifiedClaims.venue: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General, vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 271-284

verifiedClaims.claim: Elizabeth Gardner died in 1988, roughly nine months into a five-year fellowship at the University of Edinburgh, having produced her work on disordered systems and neural networks before the age of 30 while she was ill with cancer, which she chose to bear quietly. Her 1985 work on disordered systems contained the first description of what is now called the Gardner transition.
verifiedClaims.people: Elizabeth Gardner
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Edinburgh
verifiedClaims.venue: University of Edinburgh, Higgs Centre for Theoretical Physics — International Women's Day 2022 feature

verifiedClaims.claim: Haim Sompolinsky, Naftali Tishby and H. Sebastian Seung showed with equilibrium statistical mechanics that when the training error is a smooth function of continuously varying weights the generalization error decays asymptotically as the inverse of the number of examples, but that for networks with discrete weights the generalization error can undergo a discontinuous transition to perfect generalization — a first-order phase transition in learning itself.
verifiedClaims.people: Haim Sompolinsky, Naftali Tishby, Hyunjune Sebastian Seung
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review Letters, vol. 65, no. 13, pp. 1683-1686

verifiedClaims.claim: Géza Györgyi showed that a perceptron with binary synaptic weights learning from examples undergoes a first-order transition at a critical number of examples: below it the generalization error reaches a minimal positive value, and at the transition the network abruptly freezes into the state of the teacher perceptron with error identically zero. This is the cleanest early example of an all-or-nothing learning transition.
verifiedClaims.people: Géza Györgyi
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review A, vol. 41, no. 12, pp. 7097-7100

verifiedClaims.claim: H. Sebastian Seung, Haim Sompolinsky and Naftali Tishby gave the definitive statistical-mechanical treatment of learning from examples in feedforward networks, treating stochastic training as sampling from a Gibbs distribution over weights at an effective temperature. Smooth networks obey an inverse power-law learning curve; unrealizable rules can produce spin-glass phases with many degenerate minima; and nonsmooth networks display qualitatively different, sometimes discontinuous, learning curves.
verifiedClaims.people: Hyunjune Sebastian Seung, Haim Sompolinsky, Naftali Tishby
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review A, vol. 45, no. 8, pp. 6056-6091

verifiedClaims.claim: Timothy L. H. Watkin, Albrecht Rau and Michael Biehl wrote the standard review of the statistical mechanics of learning a rule, framing supervised learning as an inverse problem in a strongly interacting disordered system analogous to a spin glass and consolidating the replica-method learning-curve results of the preceding decade.
verifiedClaims.people: Timothy L. H. Watkin, Albrecht Rau, Michael Biehl
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Oxford
verifiedClaims.venue: Reviews of Modern Physics, vol. 65, no. 2, pp. 499-556

verifiedClaims.claim: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2024 was awarded jointly to John J. Hopfield (Princeton University) and Geoffrey E. Hinton (University of Toronto) 'for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks'. The Nobel committee's own framing credits Hopfield with a network described in a manner equivalent to the energy of a physical spin system, and credits Hinton with using tools from statistical physics in 1983-1985 to create the Boltzmann machine. Hopfield was born in 1933 in Chicago and received his PhD from Cornell University in 1958; Hinton was born in 1947 in London and received his PhD from the University of Edinburgh in 1978.
verifiedClaims.people: John J. Hopfield, Geoffrey E. Hinton
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Princeton University (Hopfield); University of Toronto (Hinton)
verifiedClaims.venue: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Nobel Prize in Physics 2024

verifiedClaims.claim: Dmitry Krotov and John J. Hopfield introduced dense associative memory, replacing the quadratic Hopfield energy with a higher-order polynomial or rapidly growing interaction function, which raises storage capacity from linear in the number of neurons to superlinear (polynomial in the degree of the interaction). They established a duality between dense associative memory and feedforward networks with one hidden layer, and identified two operating regimes: a feature-matching regime and a prototype regime, with the crossover between them controlled by the sharpness of the energy function.
verifiedClaims.people: Dmitry Krotov, John J. Hopfield
verifiedClaims.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NeurIPS 2016), pp. 1172-1180; arXiv:1606.01164

verifiedClaims.claim: Pankaj Mehta and David J. Schwab constructed a formal mapping between Kadanoff's variational renormalization group and stacked Restricted Boltzmann Machines, arguing that successive layers of a deep network implement RG-style coarse-graining and that deep learning therefore extracts relevant features the way RG extracts relevant operators. The correspondence was illustrated on the Ising model.
verifiedClaims.people: Pankaj Mehta, David J. Schwab
verifiedClaims.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:1410.3831 [stat.ML]

verifiedClaims.claim: Maciej Koch-Janusz and Zohar Ringel challenged the assumption that ordinary RBM training performs renormalization, and instead built a neural network that maximizes real-space mutual information between coarse-grained blocks and their environment in order to identify the relevant degrees of freedom and iterate RG steps without prior knowledge of the system; the method recovers the Ising critical exponent in one and two dimensions.
verifiedClaims.people: Maciej Koch-Janusz, Zohar Ringel
verifiedClaims.venue: Nature Physics, vol. 14, no. 6, pp. 578-582 (arXiv:1704.06279, 2017)

verifiedClaims.claim: Ellen de Mello Koch, Robert de Mello Koch and Ling Cheng tested the RG/deep-learning correspondence empirically by comparing a single layer of an RBM trained on the Ising model to a single step of RG flow, and constructed observables that expose important differences between renormalization group flow and deep learning — a direct empirical check on the 'exact mapping' claim.
verifiedClaims.people: Ellen de Mello Koch, Robert de Mello Koch, Ling Cheng
verifiedClaims.venue: IEEE Access, vol. 8 (arXiv:1906.05212, 2019)

verifiedClaims.claim: Aurélien Decelle, Florent Krzakala, Cristopher Moore and Lenka Zdeborová used the cavity method to obtain an asymptotically exact phase diagram for community detection in the stochastic block model, establishing a detectability/undetectability transition below which no algorithm can recover communities better than chance, and a separate easy/hard transition where belief propagation fails while the information-theoretic solution still exists. This is the canonical statistical-to-computational gap in inference.
verifiedClaims.people: Aurélien Decelle, Florent Krzakala, Cristopher Moore, Lenka Zdeborová
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review E, vol. 84, no. 6, art. 066106 (arXiv:1109.3041)

verifiedClaims.claim: Lenka Zdeborová and Florent Krzakala wrote the definitive review of the statistical physics of inference, systematizing the thresholds that separate regimes where inference is impossible, possible-but-computationally-hard, and easy — and connecting spin-glass concepts (clustering, condensation, replica symmetry breaking) to message-passing algorithms across signal processing, learning and community detection.
verifiedClaims.people: Lenka Zdeborová, Florent Krzakala
verifiedClaims.venue: Advances in Physics, vol. 65, no. 5, pp. 453-552 (arXiv:1511.02476, 2015)

verifiedClaims.claim: Jean Barbier, Florent Krzakala, Nicolas Macris, Léo Miolane and Lenka Zdeborová rigorously proved decades-old statistical-physics conjectures for the optimal estimation error in high-dimensional generalized linear models with random data matrices, and characterized exactly the parameter regions where the generalized approximate message-passing algorithm attains that optimum — thereby making the boundary between the 'hard' and 'easy' phases of learning a theorem rather than a conjecture.
verifiedClaims.people: Jean Barbier, Florent Krzakala, Nicolas Macris, Léo Miolane, Lenka Zdeborová
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 116, no. 12, pp. 5451-5460 (arXiv:1708.03395, 2017)

verifiedClaims.claim: Lenka Zdeborová argued in a Nature Physics commentary that understanding deep learning is also a job for physicists, making the case that the tools built for disordered systems — replica calculations, message passing, phase diagrams — are the natural instruments for explaining why deep networks generalize.
verifiedClaims.people: Lenka Zdeborová
verifiedClaims.venue: Nature Physics, vol. 16, pp. 602-604

verifiedClaims.claim: Mikhail Belkin, Daniel Hsu, Siyuan Ma and Soumik Mandal identified the 'double descent' risk curve: as model capacity grows, test error first follows the classical U-shaped bias-variance curve, peaks sharply at the interpolation threshold where the model exactly fits the training data, and then descends again as capacity increases further, often to a lower error than the classical optimum. The peak sits precisely at the transition point between the underparametrized and overparametrized regimes.
verifiedClaims.people: Mikhail Belkin, Daniel Hsu, Siyuan Ma, Soumik Mandal
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 116, no. 32, pp. 15849-15854 (arXiv:1812.11118, 2018)

verifiedClaims.claim: Preetum Nakkiran, Gal Kaplun, Yamini Bansal, Tristan Yang, Boaz Barak and Ilya Sutskever demonstrated double descent empirically across modern deep learning tasks and showed it occurs not only as a function of model size but also as a function of training epochs. They defined 'effective model complexity' to unify the two, and identified regimes in which increasing — even quadrupling — the number of training samples actively hurts test performance.
verifiedClaims.people: Preetum Nakkiran, Gal Kaplun, Yamini Bansal, Tristan Yang, Boaz Barak, Ilya Sutskever
verifiedClaims.venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2020; journal version Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment, vol. 2021, art. 124003 (arXiv:1912.02292, 2019)

verifiedClaims.claim: Mario Geiger, Stefano Spigler, Stéphane d'Ascoli, Levent Sagun, Marco Baity-Jesi, Giulio Biroli and Matthieu Wyart proposed that the loss landscape of a deep network is governed by a jamming transition analogous to that of repulsive particles: a sharp phase boundary in the number of parameters separates an underparametrized regime where the training data cannot be fitted from an overparametrized regime where it can, with characteristic critical behaviour in the Hessian spectrum near the transition. They also found that the capacity of fully connected networks to memorize random data is independent of depth.
verifiedClaims.people: Mario Geiger, Stefano Spigler, Stéphane d'Ascoli, Levent Sagun, Marco Baity-Jesi, Giulio Biroli, Matthieu Wyart
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review E, vol. 100, art. 012115 (arXiv:1809.09349, 2018)

verifiedClaims.claim: Stefano Spigler, Mario Geiger, Stéphane d'Ascoli, Levent Sagun, Giulio Biroli and Matthieu Wyart showed that the jamming transition from under- to over-parametrization directly controls generalization: as network width grows, the test error decays, then rises to a cusp exactly at the transition, then slowly decays again. Classical overfitting is localized around the jamming point, and early stopping removes the cusp entirely — connecting the physics of jamming to the double-descent peak.
verifiedClaims.people: Stefano Spigler, Mario Geiger, Stéphane d'Ascoli, Levent Sagun, Giulio Biroli, Matthieu Wyart
verifiedClaims.venue: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical, vol. 52, art. 474001 (arXiv:1810.09665, 2018)

verifiedClaims.claim: Alethea Power, Yuri Burda, Harri Edwards, Igor Babuschkin and Vedant Misra reported 'grokking': neural networks trained on small algorithmically generated datasets first memorize the training set with chance-level validation accuracy, and then, after a long plateau of continued training far past the point of overfitting, abruptly jump to near-perfect generalization. Smaller training sets require progressively more optimization before this jump occurs.
verifiedClaims.people: Alethea Power, Yuri Burda, Harri Edwards, Igor Babuschkin, Vedant Misra
verifiedClaims.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2201.02177 [cs.LG], submitted 6 January 2022

verifiedClaims.claim: Neel Nanda, Lawrence Chan, Tom Lieberum, Jess Smith and Jacob Steinhardt reverse-engineered grokking in small transformers trained on modular addition, showing the network learns to compute discrete Fourier transforms and use trigonometric identities to turn addition into rotation on a circle. Defining progress measures from that mechanism, they split training into three continuous phases — memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup — demonstrating that the apparently abrupt transition in test accuracy is the visible surface of a smooth underlying reorganization.
verifiedClaims.people: Neel Nanda, Lawrence Chan, Tom Lieberum, Jess Smith, Jacob Steinhardt
verifiedClaims.venue: The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2023), oral presentation (arXiv:2301.05217)

verifiedClaims.claim: Jason Wei and sixteen coauthors defined an 'emergent ability' of a large language model as one that is not present in smaller models but is present in larger ones, and therefore cannot be predicted by extrapolating the performance curve of smaller models. They catalogued dozens of tasks on which performance stays at random baseline until a critical model scale and then rises sharply.
verifiedClaims.people: Jason Wei, Yi Tay, Rishi Bommasani, Colin Raffel, Barret Zoph, Sebastian Borgeaud, Dani Yogatama, Maarten Bosma, Denny Zhou, Donald Metzler, Ed H. Chi, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Oriol Vinyals, Percy Liang, Jeff Dean, William Fedus
verifiedClaims.venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2022 (arXiv:2206.07682, submitted 15 June 2022)

verifiedClaims.claim: Rylan Schaeffer, Brando Miranda and Sanmi Koyejo argued that emergent abilities are an artifact of metric choice rather than a change in model behaviour: nonlinear or discontinuous metrics (such as exact-match accuracy) manufacture apparent sharp transitions, while linear or continuous metrics on the same models and outputs yield smooth, predictable improvement. They supported this with controlled experiments on GPT-3/InstructGPT, a meta-analysis of BIG-Bench tasks, and a demonstration that emergence can be induced at will in vision models by switching metrics.
verifiedClaims.people: Rylan Schaeffer, Brando Miranda, Sanmi Koyejo
verifiedClaims.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023) (arXiv:2304.15004, submitted 28 April 2023)

verifiedClaims.claim: The Schaeffer-Miranda-Koyejo rebuttal to emergent abilities received a NeurIPS 2023 outstanding paper award, which is why the 'mirage' framing became the standard counterweight to Wei et al. in subsequent discussion.
verifiedClaims.people: Rylan Schaeffer, Brando Miranda, Sanmi Koyejo
verifiedClaims.venue: NeurIPS 2023 conference proceedings

verifiedClaims.claim: Kauzmann observed that extrapolating the excess entropy of a supercooled liquid below its glass transition would make it fall below the crystal's entropy at a finite temperature — the 'Kauzmann paradox' / entropy crisis that motivates the idea of an underlying ideal glass transition.
verifiedClaims.people: Walter Kauzmann
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Princeton University (affiliation not verified against the primary article in this search)
verifiedClaims.venue: Chemical Reviews 43, 219-256

verifiedClaims.claim: The Adam-Gibbs relation ties relaxation time to configurational entropy via a 'cooperatively rearranging region' whose size grows as configurational entropy shrinks, yielding a form close to the empirical WLF/VFT law and predicting divergence where configurational entropy vanishes.
verifiedClaims.people: Gerald Adam; Julian H. Gibbs
verifiedClaims.affiliation: affiliation not verified in this search
verifiedClaims.venue: Journal of Chemical Physics 43, 139-146

verifiedClaims.claim: Mode-coupling theory: closed nonlinear self-consistent equations for density correlations in a simple liquid produce an ergodic-to-nonergodic (glass) bifurcation; for hard spheres the transition appears at packing fraction 0.516. MCT's sharp transition is not observed experimentally and is now read as a crossover.
verifiedClaims.people: Ulf Bengtzelius; Wolfgang Götze; Arne Sjölander
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Technische Universität München (Götze); Chalmers University of Technology, Göteborg (Bengtzelius, Sjölander) — affiliations not verified against the primary article in this search
verifiedClaims.venue: Journal of Physics C: Solid State Physics 17, 5915-5934

verifiedClaims.claim: Gardner analysed Ising spin glasses with p-spin interactions in mean field and found TWO transitions: a discontinuous one at T1 with a jump in the order parameter but no latent heat, and a lower T2 where that one-step replica-symmetry-broken phase becomes unstable to full RSB — the instability now called the Gardner transition.
verifiedClaims.people: Elizabeth Gardner
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Edinburgh
verifiedClaims.venue: Nuclear Physics B 257, 747-765

verifiedClaims.claim: Gardner computed the typical volume of the space of couplings that store p random patterns in an N-spin network — the 'Gardner volume' — establishing the statistical-mechanics theory of neural-network storage capacity. This is the direct historical bridge between the physics of disordered systems and learning theory, and the same author's name attaches to both the neural-capacity calculation and the glass transition.
verifiedClaims.people: Elizabeth Gardner
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Edinburgh
verifiedClaims.venue: Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General 21, 257-270

verifiedClaims.claim: Kirkpatrick and Thirumalai identified the dynamics of the p-spin-interaction spin-glass model with the structural glass transition, showing the mean-field p-spin model reproduces mode-coupling-like dynamical arrest — the seed of RFOT theory.
verifiedClaims.people: Theodore R. Kirkpatrick; Devarajan Thirumalai
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Maryland
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review Letters 58, 2091

verifiedClaims.claim: Random first-order transition (RFOT) theory: a scaling and droplet ('mosaic') picture of an ideal structural glass transition in which the supercooled liquid is made of glassy clusters separated by domain walls; as the ideal transition temperature is approached the entropic driving force vanishes and the cluster size diverges with exponent nu = 2/d.
verifiedClaims.people: Theodore R. Kirkpatrick; Devarajan Thirumalai; Peter G. Wolynes
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Maryland (Kirkpatrick, Thirumalai); University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (Wolynes, at the time; later Rice University)
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review A 40, 1045-1054

verifiedClaims.claim: The original jamming phase diagram. Liu and Nagel proposed that granular materials, foams, emulsions and supercooled liquids all sit on one phase diagram whose axes are temperature, applied load/stress and inverse density, so that thermal glass formation and athermal granular jamming are the same unjamming-to-jamming transition seen along different axes. NOTE: this one-page Nature article IS titled 'Jamming is not just cool any more' — it is not a separate later framing.
verifiedClaims.people: Andrea J. Liu; Sidney R. Nagel
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles (Liu, at the time; later University of Pennsylvania); James Franck Institute, University of Chicago (Nagel)
verifiedClaims.venue: Nature 396, 21-22

verifiedClaims.claim: Point J. For frictionless spheres with finite-range repulsion at zero temperature and zero applied stress, each configuration jams at its own threshold packing fraction; the distribution narrows with system size and converges to random close packing. Point J behaves like a critical point with power-law scaling of contact number, pressure and elastic moduli; the exponents do not depend on dimension but do depend on the interparticle potential, and low-frequency vibrational modes proliferate near the transition.
verifiedClaims.people: Corey S. O'Hern; Leonardo E. Silbert; Andrea J. Liu; Sidney R. Nagel
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Andrea J. Liu then at UCLA; Sidney R. Nagel at the James Franck Institute, University of Chicago; O'Hern later Yale University and Silbert later Southern Illinois University Carbondale (per-author affiliations at time of publication not verified in this search)
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review E 68, 011306 (preprint arXiv:cond-mat/0304421)

verifiedClaims.claim: Review of the jamming transition and the marginally jammed solid: when a system jams it goes from flowing to rigid while its structure stays disordered on both sides, and the marginally jammed solid near point J has anomalous vibrational and elastic properties (excess low-frequency modes, diverging length scales, non-affine response).
verifiedClaims.people: Andrea J. Liu; Sidney R. Nagel
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Pennsylvania (Liu); James Franck Institute, University of Chicago (Nagel)
verifiedClaims.venue: Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics 1, 347-369

verifiedClaims.claim: Twenty-five-year retrospective on the jamming phase diagram by its authors, arguing that linking jammed granular materials with glasses has been productive for understanding a wide class of systems. This is the 'later framing' piece, distinct from the 1998 Nature original.
verifiedClaims.people: Andrea J. Liu; Sidney R. Nagel
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Pennsylvania (Liu); University of Chicago (Nagel)
verifiedClaims.venue: Nature Reviews Physics 5, 630-631

verifiedClaims.claim: The standard modern review of glass-transition theory: lays out MCT, RFOT, dynamic facilitation and free-volume/kinetically-constrained pictures side by side on a microscopic statistical-mechanics footing, plus dynamic heterogeneity, aging and soft-glassy rheology. Useful as the neutral source when a book needs to say the field has several live theories rather than one.
verifiedClaims.people: Ludovic Berthier; Giulio Biroli
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Laboratoire Charles Coulomb, Université de Montpellier and CNRS (Berthier); Institut de Physique Théorique, CEA Saclay / later Laboratoire de Physique de l'École Normale Supérieure, Paris (Biroli)
verifiedClaims.venue: Reviews of Modern Physics 83, 587-645 (preprint arXiv:1011.2578)

verifiedClaims.claim: Fractal free-energy landscapes: deep in the glass phase the landscape undergoes a 'roughness transition' in which each glass basin shatters into a fractal hierarchy of marginally stable sub-basins — the Gardner transition, carried over from spin glasses into structural glasses. This marginality is what produces isostaticity and the critical exponents (basin width, weak-force distribution, quasi-contact spread) observed at jamming, folding granular jamming into glass theory.
verifiedClaims.people: Patrick Charbonneau; Jorge Kurchan; Giorgio Parisi; Pierfrancesco Urbani; Francesco Zamponi
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Duke University (Charbonneau); École Normale Supérieure / ESPCI, Paris (Kurchan); Sapienza Università di Roma (Parisi); Institut de Physique Théorique, CEA Saclay (Urbani); École Normale Supérieure, Paris (Zamponi)
verifiedClaims.venue: Nature Communications 5, 3725 (preprint arXiv:1404.6809)

verifiedClaims.claim: First numerical detection of the Gardner transition, in the infinite-range Mari-Kurchan model, located consistently by three independent signatures: divergence of the characteristic relaxation time, divergence of the caging susceptibility, and an anomalous tail in the distribution of cage order parameters.
verifiedClaims.people: Patrick Charbonneau; Yuliang Jin; Giorgio Parisi; Corrado Rainone; Beatriz Seoane; Francesco Zamponi
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Duke University (Charbonneau); Sapienza Università di Roma (Jin, Parisi, Rainone); École Normale Supérieure, Paris (Zamponi) — per-author affiliations not verified in this search
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review E 92, 012316 (preprint arXiv:1501.07244)

verifiedClaims.claim: Experimental evidence of a Gardner phase in a real granular system: in a vibrated bidisperse 2D disk packing, repeated compression cycles on the same glass make particles pick different average vibrational positions each cycle while the neighbour structure is unchanged; the inter-cycle cage separation plateaus with increasing packing fraction while the mean-square displacement keeps falling.
verifiedClaims.people: Alexandre Seguin; Olivier Dauchot
verifiedClaims.affiliation: ESPCI Paris (Dauchot, EC2M/Gulliver); Seguin's affiliation at the time not verified in this search
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review Letters 117, 228001 (preprint arXiv:1605.00827)

verifiedClaims.claim: Authoritative review of the exact mean-field (infinite-dimensional) solution of hard spheres and what survives in finite dimensions: the dynamical (MCT-like) transition, the Gardner transition, and the jamming transition, with an explicit accounting of which predictions numerical simulations confirm and which are dimension-sensitive.
verifiedClaims.people: Patrick Charbonneau; Jorge Kurchan; Giorgio Parisi; Pierfrancesco Urbani; Francesco Zamponi
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Duke University; ENS/ESPCI Paris; Sapienza Università di Roma; CEA Saclay
verifiedClaims.venue: Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics 8, 265-288 (preprint arXiv:1605.03008)

verifiedClaims.claim: The swap Monte Carlo algorithm equilibrates realistic glass-forming liquid models beyond experimental timescales, closing an eight-order-of-magnitude gap between simulation and experiment and letting configurational entropy be measured below the experimental glass transition; the measured steep entropy decrease continues, supporting an entropy-crisis scenario.
verifiedClaims.people: Ludovic Berthier; Patrick Charbonneau; Daniele Coslovich; Andrea Ninarello; Misaki Ozawa; Sho Yaida
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Université de Montpellier and CNRS (Berthier, Coslovich, Ninarello, Ozawa); Duke University (Charbonneau, Yaida)

A key data point in the still-open dimensional-dependence question.

Replace with: '...and derived a learning rule based on the difference between unit correlations measured in a clamped phase and in a free-running phase.' corrections.claim: Amit, Gutfreund, Sompolinsky 1985, PRL 55(14):1530-1533 — replica mean-field theory of the Hopfield model at p = alpha*N; 'the first analytic proof that associative memory survives as a distinct thermodynamic phase.'
corrections.correction: Citation fully confirmed via Crossref: 'Storing Infinite Numbers of Patterns in a Spin-Glass Model of Neural Networks', Daniel J. Amit, Hanoch Gutfreund, H. Sompolinsky, Phys. Rev. Lett. 55(14), 1530-1533 (1985); DOI resolves. The word 'proof' overstates the work: the replica method with a replica-symmetric ansatz is a non-rigorous (and, in the spin-glass regime, replica-symmetry-breaking-corrected) calculation, not a proof; rigorous versions came later (e.g. Talagrand, Bovier-Gayrard). Replace 'the first analytic proof that' with 'the first analytic demonstration that' or 'the first replica-theoretic calculation showing that'. URL unchanged: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.1530

corrections.claim: Gardner and Derrida 1988, J. Phys. A 21(1):271-284 — alpha_c(K) with alpha_c(0) = 2, 'twice the Hebbian-rule capacity'.
corrections.correction: Citation fully confirmed via Crossref: 'Optimal storage properties of neural network models', E. Gardner and B. Derrida, J. Phys. A 21(1), 271-284 (1988); DOI 10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/031 resolves. The comparison is factually wrong: alpha_c = 2 is roughly fourteen times, not twice, the Hebbian capacity. The Hebbian (Hopfield) rule stores alpha_c ≈ 0.138 patterns per neuron (Amit-Gutfreund-Sompolinsky), so 2 / 0.138 ≈ 14.5. (alpha_c = 2 coincides with Cover's 1965 counting result that a perceptron with N inputs can realise 2N random dichotomies; that is the correct comparison to draw, not a factor of two over Hebb.) Replace with: '...obtaining a critical line alpha_c(K) with alpha_c(0) = 2 — the celebrated result that an optimally trained perceptron can store two patterns per weight, more than an order of magnitude above the roughly 0.138 patterns per neuron achieved by the Hebbian rule.' URL unchanged: https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/031

corrections.claim: Lin, Tegmark & Rolnick, 'Why does deep and cheap learning work so well?' — 'in its appendix presents a counterexample intended to show the Mehta-Schwab RG-to-deep-belief-network mapping is invalid'; preprint 29 Aug 2016 (arXiv v1) by Lin, Tegmark and Rolnick; final version 3 Aug 2017; published J. Stat. Phys. 2017, DOI 10.1007/s10955-017-1836-5.
corrections.correction:
TWO ERRORS — this is the item the book must not print as written.

(1) The counterexample is NOT in the appendix of the version being cited. I downloaded and text-extracted arXiv v4 (the final version, internally dated 21 July 2017, identical in content to the Journal of Statistical Physics paper): it contains ZERO occurrences of the string 'counterexample', and its only appendix is 'Appendix A: The polynomial no-flattening theorem'. The RG critique that survives into the published paper is main-text Section III.5 'Distillation and renormalization', which says only: 'Although the connection between RG and machine learning has been studied or alluded to repeatedly [...Mehta and Schwab 2014...], there are significant misconceptions in the literature concerning the connection which we will now attempt to clear up.' The explicit counterexample was REMOVED before publication. It existed only in the 2016 preprint versions: in v1 (internally dated 31 August 2016) it is appendix section V.A, titled 'Why matching partition functions do not imply matching probability distributions', introduced in the main text as 'Appendix A, where we construct a counter-example to a recent claim [32] that a so-called "exact" RG is equiv[alent]...'; in the 29 September 2016 version it had been renumbered to 'Appendix B: Why renormalization is not unsupervised learning'.

(2) The 2016 preprint has only TWO authors. Both the v1 PDF (31 Aug 2016) and the 29 Sept 2016 PDF carry the byline 'Henry W. Lin and Max Tegmark' (Harvard Physics; MIT Physics & MIT Kavli Institute). David Rolnick appears only from the 2017 revision onward, with 'Dept. of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology'.

ACCURATE TEXT: 'Henry W. Lin and Max Tegmark, "Why does deep and cheap learning work so well?", arXiv:1608.08225v1 (29 August 2016), Appendix A. Published, with David Rolnick added as third author and the counterexample appendix removed, as Henry W. Lin, Max Tegmark and David Rolnick, "Why Does Deep and Cheap Learning Work So Well?", Journal of Statistical Physics 168(6), 1223-1247 (2017), DOI 10.1007/s10955-017-1836-5.' Volume/issue/pages verified via Crossref, and independently corroborated by the bibliography of Mehta et al., Physics Reports 810 (2019). URL for the preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.08225v1 ; for the published version: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10955-017-1836-5

corrections.correction:
All substantive content verified — both quotations are verbatim exact, the four-author list and order are correct, Robert de Mello Koch is confirmed absent, and the arXiv metadata typo 'Ellen de Melllo Koch' (three l's) is confirmed present. Two refinements:

(1) TITLE DIFFERS BETWEEN PREPRINT AND JOURNAL, which the dossier did not flag. Crossref for DOI 10.1103/PhysRevE.102.013307 gives the published title as 'Short-sighted deep learning' (HYPHENATED); the arXiv title is 'Short sighted deep learning' (unhyphenated). Cite the hyphenated form against the Phys. Rev. E venue.

(2) The dossier's open question about the published spelling is resolved: Crossref lists the published authors as 'Ellen de Mello Koch, Anita de Mello Koch, Nicholas Kastanos, Ling Cheng' — correctly spelled, two l's. The three-l form is an arXiv-only defect and must be hand-corrected in any auto-generated BibTeX.

corrections.claim: Mehta, Bukov, Wang, Day, Richardson, Fisher & Schwab, 'A high-bias, low-variance introduction to Machine Learning for physicists', Physics Reports 810, 1-124 (2019), arXiv:1803.08823 — 'useful as the place where the two authors restate the RBM/RG position in a peer-reviewed venue after the Lin-Tegmark exchange'.
corrections.correction:
The bibliographic data is exactly right; the CHARACTERIZATION IS NOT SUPPORTED and must not be printed as written.

Bibliography verified: seven authors in the stated order (Pankaj Mehta, Marin Bukov, Ching-Hao Wang, Alexandre G. R. Day, Clint Richardson, Charles K. Fisher, David J. Schwab), journal_ref 'Physics Reports 810 (2019) 1-124', DOI 10.1016/j.physrep.2019.03.001, v1 2018-03-23, v3 2019-05-27, 122 pages, 78 figures, 20 Python notebooks.

But I downloaded and text-extracted the full 116-page v3 and searched it: 'renormalization' appears only EIGHT times, of which five are bibliography entries and two are generic statistical-physics background. There is exactly ONE substantive mention of the mapping, in the deep Boltzmann machine discussion, and it is a soft aside, not a restatement: 'This basic logic is reminiscent of renormalization procedures that seek to decorrelate layers at each step (Li and Wang, 2018; Mehta and Schwab, 2014; Vidal, 2007).' Mehta & Schwab 2014 is cited there alongside two unrelated works and nowhere defended. Lin, Tegmark and Rolnick (2017) appears ONLY in the reference list, never in the body; Schwab & Mehta's 2016 comment is not cited at all; Koch-Janusz and Ringel (2017) appears only in the reference list. The review contains no section on RG and deep learning and takes no position on the dispute.

ACCURATE TEXT: 'Mehta and Schwab's later co-authored review makes only one passing reference to the connection, calling the layer-by-layer decorrelation of a deep Boltzmann machine "reminiscent of renormalization procedures"; it neither restates nor defends the 2014 mapping, and does not engage the Lin-Tegmark exchange.' Cite as Pankaj Mehta, Marin Bukov, Ching-Hao Wang, Alexandre G. R. Day, Clint Richardson, Charles K. Fisher and David J. Schwab, 'A high-bias, low-variance introduction to Machine Learning for physicists', Physics Reports 810, 1-124 (2019), DOI 10.1016/j.physrep.2019.03.001. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physrep.2019.03.001 . A consequence for the book: there appears to be NO peer-reviewed venue in which Mehta and Schwab restate the RG position after 2016, which strengthens rather than weakens the dossier's warning about the unpublished comment.

corrections.claim: Kelsie Taylor, 'A Deep Dive into the Connections Between the Renormalization Group and Deep Learning in the Ising Model', arXiv:2308.11075 (21 Aug 2023), Caltech thesis, DOI 10.7907/ztpg-z092; RG flow successfully learned for the 1D case but quantitative inconsistencies when comparing RBM weight layers to spin renormalization in the nearest-neighbour system.
corrections.correction:
Content verified; the description of the document type understates what it is and should be sharpened.

Verified from arXiv: single author Kelsie Taylor, published 2023-08-21, single version, DOI 10.7907/ztpg-z092. Abstract confirms both reported findings verbatim: 'For the 1D Ising model, we successfully used Adam optimization on a correlation length loss function to learn the group flow, yielding results consistent with the analytical model for infinite N' and 'we directly compared the weights of each layer from the learning to Ising spin renormalization, but found quantitative inconsistencies for the simple case of nearest-neighbor Ising models.'

CORRECTION: the comments field reads '103 pages, 87 figures, Senior Thesis, Advisors: Maria Spiropulu and Joseph Lykken'. This is an UNDERGRADUATE senior thesis, not a doctoral one. 'A Caltech thesis' will be read by most readers as a PhD thesis and overstates the source's weight. Also note the Caltech affiliation, which the dossier marked as inferred from the DOI prefix, is confirmed by the named advisors (both Caltech/Fermilab).

ACCURATE TEXT: 'Kelsie Taylor, "A Deep Dive into the Connections Between the Renormalization Group and Deep Learning in the Ising Model", Caltech senior thesis, 2023, arXiv:2308.11075, DOI 10.7907/ztpg-z092.' URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.11075
